standard.title: Science in Daily Life
standard.description: describe how people use science in their daily lives, including using patterns to make scientific predictions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have not yet examined science as a human activity used in daily life or connected the idea of patterns to prediction.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe examples of how people — including themselves, community members and First Nations Australians — use science knowledge and observed patterns to make decisions and predictions in everyday life.

nodes.label: People use science knowledge in everyday decisions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe at least two examples of how people use science knowledge in their daily lives, explaining what knowledge is being used and why.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe two examples of people using science knowledge in daily life, identifying the science knowledge used in each.
nodes.typical_width: Students identify and describe how farmers, gardeners, ecologists, engineers and families use science knowledge in daily decisions — plant care, weather planning, force use in cooking and tools, habitat design — and connect these examples to specific science concepts.
wider: Learning from farmers, bush care volunteers, gardeners or nursery owners about how they observe plant and animal needs and design habitats — examining professional science use
Investigating how First Nations Australians use science to meet needs including food, water supply and shelter
Exploring how engineers use knowledge of forces to create playground equipment or toys — connecting force concepts to design (AC9S1U03)
nodes.hinge_reason: N2's pattern-based prediction concept requires students to have first established that people use science knowledge in daily life — without this foundation, connecting patterns to prediction in N2 lacks meaningful grounding.
success_criteria: Describes two examples of people using science knowledge in daily life
Identifies the science knowledge being used in each example

nodes.label: Patterns help people make scientific predictions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe how observing patterns in nature (weather, seasons, animal behaviour) allows people to make predictions that guide decisions.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe one pattern in nature and one prediction that people make based on that pattern.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe multiple examples of pattern-based prediction — weather forecasting, seasonal resource gathering, animal behaviour prediction — and explain how the pattern is observed and used to make the prediction.
wider: Recognising how First Nations Australians use changes in the landscape and sky to answer questions about when to gather certain resources — examining long-term observational pattern knowledge
Sharing examples of how students have used science knowledge at home — weather forecasts, seasonal clothing, observing weather patterns before family events
Learning from local ecologists or wildlife carers about observing animal behaviour patterns to design habitat supports

response_modes.reason: First Nations pattern-based resource timing and personal home examples provide culturally rich and personally connected directions. Encountering pattern-based prediction across multiple contexts — ecological, cultural, domestic — builds a more complete and generalisable model.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations pattern-based resource timing provides a culturally rich and ecologically sophisticated direction. Personal examples from home connect the concept to the student's own lived experience.
success_criteria: Explains how observing that pattern helps people make a prediction or decision
